transcript.text:
I've started a prediction project to find which customers are most likely to leave next.

To build it, DCLab needs a table of your customers. It should include past customers who have left and ones who stayed, so the model can learn what leaving looks like. Details like how long they've been a customer, what they buy, how often they buy, and any support issues all help.

Share that table when you're ready, and we'll go from there.
hi, we keep losing customers every month and i dont know what to do about it

That sounds frustrating, especially when it keeps happening month after month. To make sure I picture it right: what does "losing" a customer look like in your business? Do they cancel a subscription or contract, or do they just quietly stop buying?
They cancel. We sell home internet on a monthly subscription, so they just stop paying and leave. Roughly 3 out of every 100 do it each month.

Thanks, that's clear: monthly home internet subscribers who stop paying and leave, about 3 in 100 each month. Suppose you could see which customers are likely to leave, or why they leave. What could you actually do with that today, like calling them, offering a discount, or fixing something in the service? And who on your team would act on it?

Mostly I'd want to call them before they go, I think. There are three of us in the care team and we work off a call list in Excel. Maybe offer them something to stay, but I'm not sure what would work. I just know some of them complain before they leave.

That helps: a care team of three calling people from an Excel list before they cancel. Since you can only make so many calls, the big question is who goes on that list. Do you have a customer table, something that shows each subscriber and whether and when they cancelled? And if complaints are recorded anywhere, tell me where, since you mentioned some customers complain before they leave.

Yes, we have a billing system and I can export it to Excel. It has customer number, start date, plan, monthly bill, how many support calls they've made, and whether they left. I haven't sent it yet. I think the complaints are in the support call count, but I'm not sure what else is written down. Is that enough to start?

Yes, that's enough to start. A billing export with a plan, a monthly bill, support calls and a "left" flag is usually enough to work out which customers look most like the ones who cancelled, and that would give your care team a call list. Could you export it and share it here? If there's any column showing the date someone left, please keep it in. I'll look at what's in it before we decide anything.
ok. it's just the billing export, so no names, only customer numbers. how do i send it to you? can i paste it here or does it need to be a file?

Please share it as a file rather than pasting it, because the Excel export as it is (or a CSV) keeps every row and column intact. Customer numbers only is fine, and it's better that way. Please include all your customers, the ones still with you as well as the ones who left, because the work depends on comparing the two groups. When you open the export, does "left" show only as yes/no, or is there also a date when they left?
Not sure, I'd have to open it and look. I think it's just yes or no for left, but I don't know if there's a date. Can I attach the file here, or is there another way to send it?

You don't need to check anything first. Attach the Excel file as it is (a CSV is fine too), and I'll look at the columns myself, including whether "left" has a date. I'm working on the guess that it's only yes/no, and I'll correct that if the file shows otherwise. I can't see your screen, so I can't tell you exactly where the button is. It's usually an attach or upload option next to where you type. Can you find it and send the file over? If you don't see one, tell me what's on your screen and we'll sort it out.
I don't see an attach button, only the box I type in. Can I copy some of it in here instead? It's a lot of customers, so I'm not sure that works.

Pasting a few rows isn't a good basis for this. A small piece can't show who tends to leave, and with only about 3 in 100 cancelling, leavers would barely show up in it. I'd want the whole export. I also can't see your screen, so I can't tell you how to upload it. Look for an upload option elsewhere on the page, or ask whoever set this up for you. You don't have to wait on that to get started. Here are three ways forward. The first two need the file, and the third can start now. Which one fits best?

I'll start by looking at the columns in your table.

I've started a prediction project. Your table has a `churned_next_month` column with 1,200 customers, so DCLab can learn from it which members tend to cancel. It will use columns like plan, tenure, monthly spend, segment and recent support tickets.

A weekly report needs a model that scores members first, so the model comes first. Once it's built, we can set up the weekly report listing the members most likely to cancel.

I haven't set up the weekly schedule yet. I'll do that after we've checked how well the model predicts.
need a weekly report of members likely to cancel next month. can you set that up [shares customers.csv]

Got it: you want a weekly list of members who are likely to cancel next month, and I see your table has a churned_next_month column, so I'm guessing that's how you record who left. Is that right? When the list lands each week, who will look at it and what will they do for the members on it (call them, offer a discount, something else)?

Yes, churned_next_month is 1 if they left the following month. 14 club managers read it each week. They pick about 20 members each and offer a free personal training session to keep them. I figured this was just a filtered report, so tell me if it needs more than that.

Thanks, that helps. It does need more than a filter, though. `churned_next_month` is only filled in after the month is over. If you filtered on it, you'd get members who have already left. To list members who are *likely* to leave, DCLab has to learn from past members which signs came before a cancellation. Then it can score the members you have now. Here are three ways to go, from most to least work. For the 14 managers picking about 20 members each, I'd start with the first.

choices.title: Weekly risk list from a prediction model
choices.what: DCLab learns from your past members which ones left (churned_next_month) and which signs came before it (tenure_months, monthly_spend, support_tickets_90d, plan, segment, city). It then gives each current member a risk score, and the weekly report ranks members by risk so each manager can take their top ~20.

choices.what: A weekly report that filters members by rules you choose, for example short tenure_months or many support_tickets_90d, sorted so managers can pick 20 each.

transcript.text: The prediction model is now under way. Here is what happens next. - **Learning from history:** DCLab studies your 1,200 members and how `churned_next_month` turned out for each. It looks at signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend and support tickets in the last 90 days. `customer_id` is only a label, so it isn't used as a sign. - **Checking it works:** DCLab keeps some members out of the learning and tests the model on them. You will see how well it picks out the members who really left before you rely on it. - **What you get:** a ranked list of members by how likely they are to cancel next month, with the riskiest first. That suits managers who each pick about 20 members for the free training session. I'm assuming that the current table is your history and that each week you'll give DCLab a fresh export of current members with the same columns. Tell me if that's wrong. I also noticed the table has no club column, only `city`. To give each of the 14 managers their own members, we'll need a way to tell which club a member belongs to. This doesn't hold up the model. We can sort it out when the weekly list is set up.

transcript.text: need a late-delivery model. baseline first. go

I've started a late-delivery prediction project. It will predict whether each new delivery is likely to be late. We'll build a simple baseline model first, so you have a reference score. Any later, fancier model will need to beat that score.

To set it up, I need a few things from you:
1. **Your delivery table.** This is the data with one row per delivery.
2. **What counts as "late."** Is there a column that says so, or should it be calculated from promised and actual delivery dates?
3. **Information available at prediction time.** For example, carrier, distance, order size and ship date. Tell me if any columns are only known after delivery, so we leave them out.

Share the table and I'll start on the baseline.

Table is in our warehouse, not uploaded yet. Columns: parcel_id, dispatch_time, depot, postcode, weight, driver_id, planned_route_km, actual_delivery_time, late. Label is the existing late flag (about 5% positive). Features: dispatch_time, depot, postcode, weight, driver_id, planned_route_km. Drop parcel_id and actual_delivery_time. Scores needed by 6am dispatch. Planners can re-route about 150 parcels a day, so evaluate on the top 150 per day.

Thanks, that's enough to set up the baseline. I can't see your warehouse table yet, so I'll work from your column list until it's in DCLab. The plan:

**Setup**
- **Label:** the existing `late` flag, with about 5% late.
- **Features:** `dispatch_time`, `depot`, `postcode`, `weight`, `driver_id`, `planned_route_km`.
- **Dropped:** `parcel_id` and `actual_delivery_time`. The delivery time is only known after the fact, so keeping it would make the scores look better than they really are.

**Baseline**
- A simple model, plus a no-model reference that ranks parcels by each depot's past late rate. A later model has to beat both.

**How we'll score it**
- **Time-based split:** train on earlier days and test on later ones. A random split would let the model peek at the future.
- **Top 150 per day:** for each test day, take the 150 highest-scored parcels. We'll report how many of them were actually late, and what share of that day's late parcels they cover. Picking 150 parcels at random would catch about 5% of them, so that's the floor to compare against.

**Questions**
1. **Scoring time:** is `dispatch_time` known when you score at 6am, or is it only recorded when the parcel leaves the depot? If it's recorded later, I'll use the planned dispatch time or drop it.
2. **Driver:** is `driver_id` assigned by 6am? If drivers are assigned after scoring, I'll drop it.
3. **Volume:** roughly how many parcels go out per day, and how many months of history do you have? If you dispatch only a few hundred a day, the top 150 is a very different test than if you dispatch thousands.
4. **Getting the table in:** I can't pull from your warehouse myself. Please upload an extract or connect the table in DCLab. Once it's there, I'll check the columns before training.

Not sure on 1-3. Dispatch_time and driver_id: I'll check in the warehouse whether they're set before 6am. Volume: I'll pull the daily count from the table. Get the extract into DCLab and run the baseline. I want to see the top-150 numbers.

I can't pull the extract from your warehouse myself, and nothing has been trained yet. I don't have a connection to it, so you'll need to upload the file or connect the table in DCLab. Once it's there, I'll run the baseline and show you the top-150 numbers.

**What to put in the extract**
- All nine columns, so I can check each one before training.
- The full history you have, or at least several months. The test needs later days held out.
- One row per parcel. Please check that `parcel_id` has no duplicates.
- Dispatch dates as real timestamps, not text. The day-by-day split depends on them.

**While you're in the warehouse**
- Pull the daily parcel count too. It can be a separate small query. It tells us whether "top 150" means the top 5% of a day or the top 50%.
- Check whether `dispatch_time` and `driver_id` are set before 6am.

**How I'll handle the open questions**
I'll train the baseline two ways: with all six features, and without `dispatch_time` and `driver_id`. You'll see both top-150 results side by side. If the two features turn out not to be known by 6am, you'll already have a score you can use. If they are, you'll see how much they add.

Send the extract when it's ready.
need a late-delivery model. baseline first. go

Understood: a model that predicts which deliveries will arrive late, with a simple baseline first so we know what any model has to beat. I don't see a table yet. Do you have past deliveries with a record of which ones were late, and can you share it here?

Yes, I have past deliveries with a late flag. The shipments table is in our warehouse, not uploaded yet. Columns: parcel_id, dispatch_time, depot, postcode, weight, driver_id, planned_route_km, actual_delivery_time, late. Late rate is about 5%. actual_delivery_time and anything recorded after dispatch must stay out of the features. Planners re-route about 150 parcels a day, and scores need to be ready by 6 am dispatch. Which format do you want for the baseline, and what do you need from me to get started?

Thanks, that's clear: planners re-route about 150 parcels a day from scores ready by 6 am, and actual_delivery_time and anything recorded after dispatch stay out of the features. The format of the baseline isn't something you need to choose. I'll set it up as a simple benchmark, such as the overall late rate or a basic rule by depot. It will be scored on the most recent dispatches that the model doesn't see. What I need from you is the table. Can you export an extract of the shipments table and share it here, with all the columns you listed? It should cover as many months of dispatch_time as you can, so the test period is recent. If you can't export it, tell me what's in the way and we'll work out another route.

Not uploading the table yet. Skip the explanation. Give me the baseline you'd run on my columns as SQL or Python I can execute on the warehouse side, with the late-rate benchmark and a split by dispatch_time so the test set is the latest dispatches. Also list which columns you'd exclude as leakage.

Here is a script for your warehouse. It's written in generic SQL, so you may need to adjust the interval syntax for your dialect. I haven't run it against your data. Set `{test_days}` to the length of the test window you want, in days. ```sql
WITH cut AS (
  SELECT MAX(dispatch_time) - INTERVAL '{test_days} days' AS test_start FROM shipments
),
base AS (
  SELECT s.parcel_id, s.depot, s.dispatch_time,
         CAST(s.late AS INT) AS late,
         CASE WHEN s.dispatch_time >= c.test_start THEN 'test' ELSE 'train' END AS part
  FROM shipments s CROSS JOIN cut c
  WHERE s.late IS NOT NULL
),
p_all   AS (SELECT AVG(CAST(late AS FLOAT)) AS p FROM base WHERE part = 'train'),
p_depot AS (SELECT depot, AVG(CAST(late AS FLOAT)) AS p FROM base WHERE part = 'train' GROUP BY depot),
scored AS (
  SELECT b.*, a.p AS score_overall, COALESCE(d.p, a.p) AS score_depot
  FROM base b
  CROSS JOIN p_all a
  LEFT JOIN p_depot d ON d.depot = b.depot
  WHERE b.part = 'test'
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY CAST(dispatch_time AS DATE)
           ORDER BY score_depot DESC, parcel_id) AS rn
  FROM scored
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                                            AS test_rows,
  MAX(score_overall)                                  AS train_late_rate,   -- benchmark 1: one score for every parcel
  AVG(CAST(late AS FLOAT))                            AS test_late_rate,    -- what a random pick of 150 achieves
  AVG(CASE WHEN rn <= 150 THEN CAST(late AS FLOAT) END) AS depot_rule_precision_top150_per_day  -- benchmark 2
FROM ranked;
```

**How it works**
- **Split:** the test set is the latest dispatches, covering the last `{test_days}` days. Everything earlier is train. Every rate is computed on train only. - **Benchmarks:** the overall late rate gives every parcel the same score, so it can't rank anything. The depot rule scores each parcel with its depot's train late rate. A model has to beat the depot rule's precision on the 150 parcels picked per day. At a late rate of about 5%, accuracy tells you nothing, so I use precision at 150 per day instead. **Exclude from the features**
- `actual_delivery_time`: it's the outcome, and `late` comes from it. - `late`: it's the label. - `parcel_id`: it's an identifier and carries no signal. - Anything else in the warehouse recorded after dispatch, such as scan events, delay codes or exception flags. **Check before you include**
- `driver_id` and `planned_route_km` are safe only if they hold the values as of the 6 am scoring. If re-routing or reassignment overwrites them after dispatch, they leak. - `dispatch_time` is fine for hour and weekday features if it's the planned time known at 6 am. It isn't fine if it's a logged actual time. - Any depot or driver late-rate feature must be computed from rows before the parcel's dispatch, never from the test period. The usable feature set is `depot`, `postcode`, `weight`, and, if they pass the checks above, `driver_id`, `planned_route_km` and time-of-day or weekday from `dispatch_time`. **What happens next:** DCLab can't build or score the model without data. Paste the single result row here and I'll read it against your 5% late rate with you. When you can share an extract of the shipments table, with as many months of `dispatch_time` as possible, the model goes on top of this baseline with the same time-based split.

transcript.text: can you look at my sales data and tell me something useful [shares sales.csv]

I'll start by looking at what's in your sales table.

Your table has 2,020 orders. For each order it records the date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer. I can look at that in a few ways, so I've listed some options below.

- **Break down your sales** shows what happened, such as sales by month, region, channel or product category.
- **Find out why sales moved** looks into a business question, like why sales rose or fell or where to focus.
- **Find natural customer groups** groups customers by how they buy.
- **Build a sales dashboard** gives you a report that stays current as new orders arrive.

If you want a quick first look, I'd start with the breakdown. Pick whichever fits best. If you already have a question in mind, tell me and I'll start there.

choices.title: Break down your sales
choices.what: Totals and trends from what already happened: sales by month, region, channel and product category, and which ones are growing or shrinking.

choices.title: Find out why sales moved
choices.what: Look into a business question, such as why sales went up or down, or where to focus next, using your order data.

choices.title: Find natural customer groups
choices.what: Group your customers by how they buy (how often, how much, what they buy) to see types you might not have spotted.

choices.title: Build a sales dashboard
choices.what: A report that stays up to date with sales by date, region, channel and category as new orders come in.

transcript.text: I want to know what kinds of customers I have. We're starting a loyalty thing in March and I need to know who buys what. Can you group them that way?
transcript.pick: Find natural customer groups

transcript.text:
I've started the customer grouping project. It will look at how each customer buys in your sales data. That includes how often they order, how much they spend, and which channels, regions and product categories they use. Customers who buy in similar ways will be put in the same group.

Next, you'll be able to review the groups it finds. For each group you'll see how many customers it has and what sets it apart. That should show you which customers are your big spenders, which ones buy occasionally, and so on.
can you look at my sales data and tell me something useful [shares sales.csv]

Happy to dig in. I can see 2,020 orders with date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer, so there's a fair bit to look at. "Useful" depends on what you're trying to decide, though. Is something on your mind with the sales, like a slowdown, a region or channel you're unsure about, or where to put effort next? Or are you just curious what stands out?

I'm thinking about starting a loyalty programme in March. I want to know what kinds of customers I actually have, so I can make a few different reward levels. Not sure what the data can show for that.

That's something the data can help with. Your table has a customer_id on every order, with dates and amounts, so I can see how often each customer buys, how recently, and how much they spend, and look for natural groups from that. I'm assuming you're the one setting the levels, so tell me if someone else will use this too. What do you most want the programme to do: get occasional buyers to come back more often, reward your biggest spenders, or something else?

Mostly I want people to come back more, but I also want to reward the ones who already spend a lot. Not sure which matters more yet, that's partly why I'm asking. It's me and my store managers who'll use it, at a planning meeting in December. We launch in March and the budget is small, so it has to be simple.

Here's what I understood. You want to come back more often, but you also want to reward your big spenders, and you don't yet know which matters more. It has to be simple enough for you and your store managers to use in December, and cheap enough for a small March budget. Your table has what we need: `customer_id`, `order_date` and `amount` on each order. I'd also leave out cancelled or returned orders when I count purchases. I'll check the `status` column for that. The three options below take different routes. You could let the data suggest the groups, set simple cutoffs yourselves, or first settle which aim to focus on. Which one fits best?

choices.title: Find your natural customer groups
choices.what: DCLab looks at each customer's buying pattern (how recently they bought, how often, how much they spend in total) and finds the groups that naturally appear, then describes each group in plain words for your managers.

choices.title: Simple tiers from orders and spend, you set the cutoffs

transcript.text: I'd like to cluster our travellers from the bookings table, using lead time, channel, price and maybe nationality. Price is a string with a currency, so it needs parsing first. I'm also not sure k-means is right with mixed types. [shares bookings.csv]

I'll start by looking at the columns in your bookings table.

Your table has 1,500 bookings, and `price` is stored as text, as you said. Parsing it has to come first, so I'm starting with that. Once price is a number, we can set up the clustering.

The price-cleaning step has started. It will split `price` into an amount and a currency, so the amount can be used as a number.

- **Currencies:** If the table has more than one, the amounts can't be compared as they are. We'd need to convert them to one currency or cluster within each currency.
- **Your k-means question:** Plain k-means works on distances between numbers, so it handles channel and nationality badly. One-hot encoding them is a common workaround. Nationality has many values, so it tends to dominate the result. Methods built for mixed types, such as k-prototypes, or clustering on a mixed-type distance like Gower, usually fit better. You could also group rare nationalities into regions, or leave nationality out of the first run.
- **One row per booking:** `customer_id` is in the table, so one traveller may appear several times. Decide whether you're grouping bookings or travellers. If it's travellers, we'd first roll the bookings up to one row per customer.
- **Cancelled:** I'd leave `cancelled` out of the clustering inputs. It works better for describing the groups afterwards.

When the price step is done, I can set up the clustering on lead time, channel, price and nationality. Do you want to cluster bookings or travellers?

Yes, travellers. The product team needs to design packages for types of people, so I want one row per customer_id, not per booking. For each traveller I'd roll up: number of bookings, median lead time, median price, the share of bookings through each channel, and the share of free-cancellation bookings. Destinations and nationality can be the main profile columns for describing the groups afterwards. I'd like to test nationality both in the clustering and outside it, to see whether it drives the groups or just labels them.

On currency: the price text has a currency in it, but I'm not sure which currencies are in there. I'd expect mostly AED, but I haven't checked, so please show me the distinct currencies before we convert anything.

For the deliverable, the product team needs three themes, so I'd aim for about 3 to 6 clusters that are easy to explain. If the groups are unstable across seeds or values of k, I'd rather tell them that than force a clean story. The presentation is in three weeks, so I'd like a first pass on the price cleaning and the traveller-level table this week.

That plan works. I'll do it in order, with a stop for your decision on currency.

**1. Price cleaning (running now)**
- It splits `price` into an amount and a currency.
- It lists every distinct currency with a count of bookings, so you can check the AED assumption.
- It flags any price text it can't parse, rather than guessing.
- Nothing is converted at this stage.

**2. Currency decision (you)**
- If it's all AED, there's nothing to convert.
- If other currencies show up, you choose between converting to one currency, which needs a rate source and date, and clustering within each currency. If they are only a handful of bookings, you could also set them aside.

**3. Traveller-level table (starts once step 2 is settled)**
I'm holding this back because median price depends on the currency answer. The table will have one row per `customer_id` with:
- number of bookings
- median lead time
- median price
- share of bookings through each channel
- share of free-cancellation bookings

Destinations and nationality will be kept as profile columns, outside the clustering inputs. Cancellation will also be a profile column, as a share of each customer's bookings.

**Checks I'll run while building the table**
- **Nationality per customer:** I'll check that each `customer_id` has only one. If some have several, we'll need a rule, such as most frequent or "multiple".
- **Destinations:** Customers can book several, so I'd keep a share per destination or the top destination, rather than one value.
- **One-booking customers:** For these, "median" is just a single value and channel shares are 0 or 100%. I'll add the booking count so we can see how many travellers this affects. We may want a minimum number of bookings for the clustering.
- **Missing or duplicate IDs:** I'll count rows with a blank `customer_id` before rolling up.
- **Lead time:** I'll check that `lead_time_days` matches travel date minus booking date, and look for negative values.
- **Channel shares:** They add up to 100%, so one channel column is redundant for distance-based clustering. I'll drop one there.

**Later, once the table is approved**
- Cluster twice, once with nationality inside and once without, then compare the groups and see how much nationality changes them.
- Try k from 3 to 6.
- Re-run with different seeds, and report how stable the groups are across seeds and k. If they aren't stable, I'll say so rather than force a clean three-theme story.

This should fit your timeline: steps 1 to 3 this week, which leaves time for the clustering and for writing it up for the presentation.

Once you see the currency list, tell me how you want to handle it, and I'll build the traveller table.

I'd like to cluster our travellers from the bookings table, using lead time, channel, price and maybe nationality. Price is a string with a currency, so it needs parsing first. I'm also not sure k-means is right with mixed types. [shares bookings.csv]

So you want to group your travellers by how and when they book and what they pay, and you're weighing up how to handle price parsing and the mix of number and category columns. I've looked at the table and both are workable. The method matters less than what the groups are for. Once you have them, what do you want to do with them? For example, target different offers, change pricing, or rethink which channels you push.

None of the three you listed, really. The aim is to design new package types. Our product team is three people, and they'll pick 3 new package themes for summer 2027 based on the groups I find. So the groups need to be something they can name and sell. For each group I'd want to see the typical destinations, when they travel, lead time, price range, which channel they book through, and nationality mix, so the team can tell what the traveller wants. I'm presenting to them in 3 weeks, so I need the groups stable and explainable more than I need the cleverest method. I'm happy with clustering on lead time, channel, price and nationality if the output can be profiled that way. Does that change what you'd recommend?

Your goal does change my advice a little. It doesn't change the plan. The clustering you described still fits. Because the team has to name and sell each group, I'd use lead time, channel, price and nationality to form the groups. Destination and travel timing would then describe them. That way "typical destinations" and "when they travel" are results the team can read, not something built into the groups. DCLab would handle price parsing and the mixed column types, so you don't need to settle the k-means question up front. It would also check how stable the groups are, which matters for your presentation. I'm assuming each row is one booking, even though some customers may book more than once. I'll also check for cancelled bookings and mixed currencies before grouping. Correct me if either is wrong. Here are two ways to go:

choices.title: Cluster bookings, then profile each group
choices.what: Parse price into a number (converting currencies if there are several), then find groups from lead_time_days, channel, price and nationality. Each group is then profiled on destination and travel_date (when they travel), plus lead time, price range, channel and nationality mix. Destination and travel timing are used to describe the groups, not to form them.

choices.title: Profile the groups you already have: destination and season
choices.what: No clustering. Parse price, then describe bookings by destination and travel season (from travel_date). For each, show lead time, price range, channel and nationality mix.

transcript.text: I'll go with option 1. It matches the brief: the groups have to be nameable and sellable, and destination and travel timing should describe them, not define them. Before the run, a few points. (1) Please drop cancelled = 1 from the grouping. We want what travellers actually bought, not what they abandoned. (2) Check how many bookings each customer_id has. If a few repeat customers account for many rows, they could pull a group toward one person's habits, so I'd like a sensitivity run with one row per customer. (3) Nationality is categorical and lead_time and price are numeric, so scale the numerics and use Gower distance or one-hot encoding. Tell me which you use and why. (4) I need stability, not just a best k. Please run bootstrap resampling and several seeds, report how often each booking lands in the same group, and show silhouette only as a secondary check. (5) For the presentation, each group should show size as a share of bookings, not just as a count. Also check for anything in the data that isn't a real booking before you profile. Can you confirm which currencies appear in price?
transcript.pick: Cluster bookings, then profile each group

transcript.text: The grouping is under way. Here is what happens next. - **Preparation:** DCLab parses the `price` strings into one numeric amount. It also checks the table for mixed currencies and for cancelled bookings, using the `cancelled` column. If either is a problem, you'll see how it was handled. - **Grouping:** The groups are formed from `lead_time_days`, `channel`, price and `nationality`. DCLab handles the mix of numbers and categories, so you don't have to decide on k-means. - **Stability:** DCLab checks whether the groups hold up, so you can tell the product team how far to trust them. - **Profiles:** Each group gets a profile with its typical `destination`, the timing from `travel_date`, lead time, price range, channel and nationality mix. Destination and travel timing describe the groups. They don't form them. I'm still assuming each row is one booking, even though `customer_id` shows some travellers may appear more than once. If you'd rather group by customer, tell me and I'll change the work. You'll see the results once DCLab has run. I can't give you group counts or numbers before then.

transcript.text: are my business customers different from the normal ones?

I've started a comparison of your business customers and your other customers. It will use the data you already have, such as how much each group spends, how often they buy and how big their orders are.

If you want it to focus on something specific, tell me. Examples are revenue, repeat purchases, or which products each group buys.
are my business customers different from the normal ones?

I understand you want to know whether your business customers behave differently from your regular ones. What's behind the question for you? Is there something you're thinking of doing, like pricing, service or marketing, that depends on the answer? And what kind of difference matters most to you?

Kind of. I'm thinking about hiring someone to look after the company members, like an account manager, but I'm not sure yet. I mostly want to know what they pay, how long they stay, and how much they complain compared to freelancers. I need an answer by end of November.

Thanks, that helps a lot. So you're weighing an account manager for your company members, and you want to see how they compare with freelancers on what they pay, how long they stay and how much they complain, by the end of November. I'm assuming you're the one making the call on the hire, so tell me if someone else is. What records do you have on your customers today? For example, do you have a table with each customer, their type (company or freelancer), what they pay, when they joined or left, and their complaints?

Yes, there's a members spreadsheet from our booking software. I think it has who's a company and who's a freelancer, when they started, their plan and monthly fee, how many months they've been with us, and complaints. I haven't sent it over yet. Is that enough to start?

Yes, that sounds like enough to start: type, fee, months as a member and complaints are what a company-versus-freelancer comparison needs. I'd like to see the file before I promise anything, though, because I need to check how each of those is recorded. Could you share the spreadsheet here? One thing to tell me when you do: does it include people who have already left, or only current members? That affects how fairly we can compare how long each group stays.
Not sure about the leavers. I think it's the whole list from the booking software, but I'd have to look. How do I send it to you? Can I paste it in here or is there another way?

Pasting rows into the chat isn't ideal, because it's easy to lose columns or cut the list short. It's better to share the spreadsheet as a file, as a CSV or Excel export from the booking software. I can't see an attach button from my side, so look for the option to add or share a table in DCLab. Once it's in, I can read the column names myself, and you don't need to check the leavers question beforehand. Can you try sharing the file and tell me whether it went through?
Um, I'm not really sure how to export it from the booking software. I'll try to find the button later. Can't I just tell you the main numbers instead?

Yes, you can tell me the numbers, and we can start from there. It's a stopgap, though. I'd be working from figures you've worked out yourself, and DCLab's code hasn't checked them. One example is that the average time as a member can look quite different depending on whether people who left are counted. The spreadsheet is still the better route. Most booking tools have an "Export" or "Download" button on the members or customers list, or under "Reports". If you can't find it, the software's support can usually send you a CSV. What numbers do you have to hand today for company members and freelancers, such as how many of each, what each group pays and how long they've stayed?
I don't have the exact numbers to hand, I'd have to go through the sheet. I'll try to find the export button later today. Is there anything I can do before then?

Yes, there's a bit you can do while you look for the export. When you open the sheet, you could check three things:

1. Is there a column that says company or freelancer? 2. Are people who have left in the list, or only current members? 3. Is "complaints" a count per person, or just a yes/no? You don't have to send numbers, just jot down what you see. I'm also assuming you're the one deciding on the hire. Tell me if that's not right. The other thing you can do is think about the decision itself. Suppose the sheet shows company members pay more, stay longer or complain more than freelancers. Which of those would make you say "yes, I should hire someone for them"?

Um, I guess if company members pay more or stay longer, that would make sense for an account manager. Complaints too, maybe, I'm not sure. I'll look at the sheet later and see what's in it. Yes, I'm the one deciding on the hire.

Thanks, that's clear. You're the one deciding, and higher pay or longer stays would count in favour of an account manager. Complaints are a maybe for you. Two things are still open, so I'm treating them as assumptions. The first is that your sheet has a company/freelancer column, the monthly fee, months as a member and a complaints count. The second is that I don't yet know whether people who have left are in it. Once the file arrives I'll check both, and nothing below can finish without it. Here are three ways to go. Pick whichever suits you now, and you can switch later.

I'll note what the file has to show before we can answer your question, then give you the guidance.

Here is some guidance for while you look for the export. I can't tell you yet whether company members differ from freelancers, because that needs the file. **Finding the export**
- Open the members or customers list and look for "Export", "Download", "CSV" or "Excel". Check the "Reports" menu too. - Check the list filter. Many booking tools show only active members by default, so switch it to "All" or "Include cancelled" before you export. That also answers your leavers question. - If you can't find the button, ask the software's support: *"Please send me a CSV of all members, including former ones, with customer type, start date, plan, monthly fee, months as a member and complaints."*

**What to look at when you open the sheet**
- Is there a column for company or freelancer? - Is there a status or end-date column? If so, leavers are probably in the list. - Are complaints a count per person or just yes/no? **Reading the comparison fairly**
- If the list holds only current members, "how long they stay" will look longer for everyone. A comparison between the two groups could mislead, and I'll say so rather than overclaim. - A complaints count grows the longer someone has been a member. Complaints per month are fairer than raw totals. - For the hire, the number of company members matters as well as what each one pays. A group that pays more but is very small may not justify a salary. Once you have the file, share it in DCLab and I'll read the columns first. Then we can pick the comparison or the account manager brief from there. That leaves plenty of time before the end of November.

transcript.text:
Good choice. Here's how I'd find your costs, starting with the easiest places to look. **Where costs usually live**
- **Supplier invoices or price lists.** What you pay per item is the most important cost. If you buy or make the products, it's in those papers or emails. - **Your accounting or shop tool.** Some of these store a "cost per item" for each product. Check whether yours does. - **A spreadsheet of your own.** If you've ever worked out prices, there may already be a cost column in it. **If you can't find exact costs**
You don't need exact figures. For each category, estimate roughly what share of the sale price goes to buying or making the product. A rough percentage is enough to tell which categories earn more and which earn less. You can replace it with real numbers later. **Other costs to include**
- Shipping you pay for. - Payment fees. - Refunds and returns. Your table has a status column, and I'd leave out cancelled or returned orders. I haven't looked at what values it holds yet. **Where you'll end up**
Once you have a cost or margin for each category, profit is the sale amount minus those costs, grouped by category and week. That's the Monday view you want for your ad money. Until then, sales.csv can only show what customers paid. **What happens next**
This is guidance only, so I'm not running anything on your data yet. Your first step is to look in those three places and jot down a rough cost percentage for each category. When you have it, bring it back and we can turn it into weekly profit by category. Does that give you enough to start looking, or is there a part you'd like me to explain more?

That's a short list, not a spreadsheet of orders. To get each figure from your invoices:
- Pick two or three typical products in the category. - Compare what you paid the supplier with what customers pay you. - Use that rough share for the whole category. If you have a lot of categories, start with the few you'd actually consider advertising. With a small ad budget, those are the ones that matter most. Once you bring that list back, we can turn it into weekly profit by category. Does that make it feel more doable?

Yeah, I think so. I'll dig through my emails tonight for the supplier stuff. Probably just the main categories I spend ad money on. Do I send you the list as a message, or do I need to put it in the file?

transcript.text: Please build a dashboard on the customers table I uploaded, refreshed monthly: churn rate by plan and by city, average monthly_spend, and support tickets per customer. It's for the Monday leadership meeting of our internet provider. [shares customers.csv]

I'll check the columns in your customers table first. That way the dashboard uses the right fields.

I've started building your dashboard. Your table has everything it needs. Here is how I plan to build each number:

- **Churn rate by plan and by city:** the share of customers with `churned_next_month` set to 1, split by `plan` and by `city`.
- **Average monthly spend:** the average of `monthly_spend` across customers.
- **Support tickets per customer:** the average of `support_tickets_90d`, which counts tickets over the last 90 days. The dashboard will label it that way, so leadership doesn't read it as a monthly figure.

It will refresh monthly, and I'm keeping the layout simple for the Monday meeting.

Two things to know:
- `churned_next_month` records whether a customer left in the month after the data snapshot. Each refresh will show churn for the month after the data was captured, not the month just ended. A label like "churn in the following month" would make that clear to the room.
- The table has 1,200 customers. Some cities or plans may have only a few, and their churn rates can swing a lot. I'd show customer counts next to each rate.

Please build a dashboard on the customers table I uploaded, refreshed monthly: churn rate by plan and by city, average monthly_spend, and support tickets per customer. It's for the Monday leadership meeting of our internet provider. [shares customers.csv]

Thanks, that's clear. You want a monthly-refreshed dashboard for your Monday leadership meeting, with churn rate by plan and by city, average monthly_spend, and support tickets per customer. Your table has what I need for those: plan, city, monthly_spend, support_tickets_90d and churned_next_month. I'm assuming churned_next_month = 1 means the customer left, and that "tickets per customer" means the average of support_tickets_90d (tickets over the last 90 days). Tell me if either is wrong. What do you want leadership to decide or act on from this? For example, where to focus retention effort, or whether to change plans or pricing. The answer decides what the dashboard should put first.

Yes, both assumptions are right. churned_next_month = 1 means the customer left the following month, and support_tickets_90d is the 90-day ticket count, so the average of that column is what leadership means by tickets per customer.

Leadership uses this to decide where to focus retention and service efforts each month. They're six people at the Monday meeting, and they're not analysts. What matters most to me is that they see the same definitions and the same layout every month, so they can compare months without me rebuilding slides. The dashboard needs to refresh monthly from the customers table, and the first version has to be ready before next Monday.

I'd like the churn view to make it clear which groups carry the most churn, since that's where retention effort goes. I know the table also has segment and tenure_months, but I haven't decided yet whether leadership should see those on the first version. What would you suggest for the first screen?

Thanks, that gives me what I need on the decision: leadership uses this each month to decide where to focus retention and service effort, and the numbers have to mean the same thing every month. For the first screen, I'd suggest this. At the top, three plain headline numbers: overall churn rate, average monthly_spend, and tickets per customer. Below them, churn by plan and churn by city as ranked bars, highest first. Each bar would show the churn rate and how many customers left, so a small city with a high rate doesn't look as big as a large city that loses the most people. I'd keep segment and tenure_months off version one. Six non-analysts reading one screen will focus better with less on it, and we can add them as a second page once the first layout has settled. Does that fit what you picture? One thing I need before building: the table has no column saying which month the data is from. When it refreshes each month, will you send a fresh export of the whole customer list with the same columns, and do you want the dashboard to keep earlier months so leadership can see change from month to month?

transcript.text: the sales team wants some kind of bookings view each week, not sure what exactly [shares bookings.csv]

I'll start by looking at what's in bookings.csv, so the options I suggest fit your data.

Your table has 1,500 bookings. It includes booking date, travel date, destination, channel, price and whether each booking was cancelled. That's enough for a useful weekly view.

Since you're not sure what the sales team wants yet, here are four places to start. Pick whichever is closest.

- **Weekly dashboard:** If you already know you want something that refreshes every week, this is the one to pick.
- **Weekly numbers first:** This works well if you'd like to show the team some real figures and let them say what they want to keep.
- **Fix the price column:** Price is being read as text, not numbers. Any weekly view that shows revenue will need this cleaned up first.
- **Cancellations:** Choose this if cancellations are the team's main worry.

transcript.text: Yeah, the weekly one. It needs to be ready before Monday 9. Mostly new bookings and cancellations by destination and channel, that's what they look at.
transcript.pick: Weekly bookings dashboard

transcript.text:
I've started the weekly bookings dashboard. It's built from your bookings table and will show bookings by week. You'll be able to split them by destination, channel and nationality, with cancellations next to them.

The price column is currently read as text, so revenue figures may not add up correctly yet. You can leave revenue out of the first version, or we can clean up price first. Which would you rather do?
Leave revenue out for now, I don't think they need it this week. Also there might be some test rows in the file, I haven't cleaned those yet. Can you make sure those don't end up in the counts?

Revenue is out of the first version, so the price column won't affect anything this week.

I can't promise the test rows are excluded yet. I haven't seen any of the actual values in your file, so I can't tell which rows are tests. Before I set up the filter, I need to know how to spot them. Some common signs:

- A booking ID or customer ID that starts with something like "TEST" or "demo".
- A destination or nationality with an obvious placeholder value.
- A booking date or travel date that's clearly wrong, such as far in the past or the future.
- A price of zero, or a very odd one. Price is left out of the dashboard, but it can still help flag a test row.

Tell me which of these applies, or describe the pattern in your own words. I'll then remove those rows in a short cleanup step ahead of the dashboard, so the weekly counts only include real bookings. If you aren't sure what they look like, I can list the unusual rows first, and you can tell me which ones to drop.
the sales team wants some kind of bookings view each week, not sure what exactly [shares bookings.csv]

Thanks, I've looked at bookings.csv: it has 1,500 bookings with dates, destination, channel, nationality, price, free cancellation and a cancelled flag, so there's plenty to build a weekly view from. What I understand so far is that the sales team wants a regular weekly look at bookings. When they sit down with it on a Monday, say, what are they trying to decide or keep an eye on? It could be whether they're on track, which channels or destinations to push, or cancellations. Whatever it is, tell me in your own words.
Mostly which destinations to push that week, I guess. And whether cancellations are going up. Like new bookings and cancels by destination and channel, every week.

Thanks, that helps. As I understand it, every week the sales team wants to pick which destinations to push and see whether cancellations are rising. They want new bookings and cancels by destination and channel for that. One limit you should know about. The table says whether a booking was cancelled, but not when. Cancels will therefore count against the week the booking was made, not the week the customer cancelled. I see three ways to go. They differ in how lasting they are and in how much they decide for you. Which one fits best?

The table has no cancellation date, so a cancel counts against the week the booking was made, not the week the customer cancelled. Recent weeks may therefore look better than they are, because some of those customers haven't cancelled yet. - **"Push" means more bookings, for now.** I'm assuming a destination to push is one where bookings are growing or lagging. transcript.text: I think the second one. Each teacher keeps attendance and grades in their own Google Sheet, and they're not shared yet. I just need a simple summary by class, once a term. transcript.text: Good, I've started the analysis. I'll work out how each class has done so far. To get going, I need to know which table has your class data. It's also useful to know which numbers matter most to you, for example average grades, attendance or change over time.
is there a way to show parents how classes are doing

transcript.text:
Here's the short guide. **1. Start with the office**
- Ask whether teachers or the head need to approve sharing records, and whether the school has a rule about pupil data, even with names removed. - Ask whether the office keeps one attendance register for all classes. If it does, you may not need to collect attendance from each teacher. **2. Ask one teacher first**
- Ask for the layout only: the column headings and a few rows. - Names should be deleted or swapped for numbers before anything is sent. - Ask the teacher to make a copy of the sheet and strip it down. That way you never get access to the original. **3. Keep it at class level**
- The council only needs one attendance figure and one average grade per class, so only those should leave the teachers' hands. - Be careful with very small classes or groups. A figure can point to one child even without a name, so check this with the office. **4. Be open with the teachers**
- Tell them what it's for: comparing classes so the council can decide where the tutoring money goes. - Show them the class-level figures before the parents' council sees them. This will make them much more comfortable. **5. Check the sheets match before combining them**
- Are the headings the same? Do they cover the same time period? Is everyone grading on the same scale? - If they don't match, the sheets will need tidying first. That's normal, and it's something DCLab can help with. I'm assuming the teachers' sheets are similar enough to combine and that the school is fine with class-level figures going to the council. The office and the first sample sheet will tell you whether both hold. Once you've spoken to the office and have a sample, bring it back. I've started a dashboard for the CFO's KPI page. It will track revenue, refunds, and orders by channel. It's a reporting page that stays up to date, with no models involved.

Next I'll need to know which table or data source holds your orders, revenue, and refunds. It would also help to know how often the page should refresh and what time period it should open on, such as month to date. If you have a preferred layout, tell me that too.
cfo wants a live kpi page. revenue, refunds, orders by channel. no models

Got it: a live page for the CFO with revenue, refunds and orders split by channel, and no models, just reporting. To see what's possible, where do those numbers sit today? For example, is there one orders table with the amount, any refund and the channel on each row, or are they spread across a few systems or files?

One orders table in our Postgres warehouse: order id, date, channel, amount, status. I won't upload it. Refunds are status values in that table. Daily refresh, and it can't take more than a few days of my time. What would you build?

What will the CFO actually do with this page? Is it a daily check, or something for a regular review where a channel gets more or less budget? The answer decides which comparisons and time views go on the page.
Daily check. She wants to spot problems early and adjust weekly cash planning from it. That's enough detail. Show me what you'd build: the SQL and the page layout.

Here's what I'd build, in two sizes. The page is for a daily check. It shows yesterday against the same weekday last week, a trend by channel, and a flag when a channel's refunds or revenue move sharply. A week-to-date block feeds her cash planning. I'm assuming each order is one row and refunds are identified by status value. The SQL will have the refund statuses in one place at the top. I'm also assuming revenue is shown gross, with refunds and a net figure beside it. If either is wrong, tell me and I'll change it. Which of the two do you want me to start with?

**Table 1: basic vs. other plans**
Show customers, churned, churn rate, total `monthly_spend`, and `monthly_spend` summed over churned customers. Add that lost spend as a share of total spend.

**Table 2: ticket bands**
Start with 0, 1–2, 3–5 and 6+, with the same columns as Table 1. Merge any band with fewer than about 30 customers or about 10 churners.

**Table 3: plan × ticket band**
Show n, churned and churn rate in each cell. Also show the share of basic and non-basic customers in each band, plus average tickets by plan. That tells you directly whether basic customers file more tickets. Then read across the table in two ways:
- Within a band, compare basic with other plans.
- Within a plan, compare the bands.

**Table 4: segment, city, tenure**
- Cut each by plan and by ticket band, with n, churned and churn rate.
- Use tenure bands such as 0–6, 7–12, 13–24 and 25+ months, adjusted to the real spread.
- Group small cities into "Other".

That sounds frustrating. I can help in a few ways, depending on what's most useful right now.

Pick whichever fits best. If you're not sure, the first one is a good place to start. It looks at why visits dropped and what you can do about it.

transcript.text: Visits have dropped a lot since the app got better, from around 2,400 a month to about 1,700. I'm not sure if it will keep falling. I have the monthly numbers and a rough split by weekday in a spreadsheet. I need to decide whether to stop Saturday opening and move one teller to phone support, and I have to send a proposal to my regional manager next month.

I've started the analysis of your visit numbers. It will look at how visits have changed over time, so you can see when the drop began and where it's biggest.

If you have a table with visit data, such as dates, branch and customer type, share it. That lets the analysis use your real numbers.
fewer people coming to the branch, not sure what to do

Thanks for laying it out. If I've got it right, fewer people are coming through the branch than before, and you're unsure how to respond. Before I suggest anything, what's the decision you're facing? Is something already on the table, like changing hours, staffing, or marketing, or do you first need to understand what's going on?

Mostly staffing. I might stop opening on Saturdays and move one teller over to phone support. I have to send a proposal to my regional manager next month. I can't cut anyone, only move them. I've got rough monthly visit numbers in a spreadsheet, but I'm not sure what they show.

That helps a lot. So the choice is whether to close Saturdays and move one teller to phone support, with nobody cut, and a proposal due to your regional manager next month. I'm assuming what you need from the numbers is to see whether visits have really dropped and whether that supports the move. Tell me if I've got that wrong. Here's my question: does your spreadsheet only give a total for each month, or does it also show Saturdays separately from weekdays, or give daily detail? That decides how much we can say about Saturdays in particular. If you can share the spreadsheet, I'll look at it too.

I've got monthly visit counts, and I think there's a rough split by weekday, Saturdays included. I haven't sent it anywhere yet. I can type a few numbers in if that's easier than the whole file. Also, I want to know whether the drop will carry on, not only whether it happened.

Thanks, that's clear: you want to know if the drop is real, and whether it will keep going, because that's what your regional manager will want to see behind the Saturday move. Typing a few numbers is a good way to start. Could you type in the monthly visit counts as far back as you have them, with the Saturday figure next to each month if you've got it? Tell me roughly how many months that covers, too. That tells me how far ahead we can honestly look.

Not sure of the exact figures, they're rough. Before the app got better we were around 2,400 a month, and this year it's down to about 1,700. I think I've got this year's months in the sheet, maybe January onwards, but I'd have to check. The Saturday split is a rough guess, not counted properly. Is it enough to start with those rough numbers?

Yes, rough numbers are enough to start. Going from about 2,400 to about 1,700 a month is a big drop, and it's worth looking at properly. The limit is what we can say afterwards. Your Saturday split is a guess and you may only have a few months of this year's figures. So we can describe the drop and give a cautious view of where it's heading. We can't give a firm Saturday-specific forecast yet. I'm also assuming the drop comes from customers moving to the improved app, so it's more likely to last than to be a dip. Correct me if that's wrong. Here are three ways to go. Which one is closest to what you need for the proposal?

I've started a business brief on whether to push store or web next year. It's the right place to begin, because it frames the decision before anyone digs into the numbers.

The brief will probably look at these things:
- **Past performance:** how store and web have each done on sales, margin, and growth.
- **Cost to grow:** what it takes to win an extra dollar of sales in each channel.
- **Customers:** whether the two channels bring in different people, and whether web customers also buy in store, or the reverse.
- **Outlook:** where each channel has room to grow, and what risks come with each.

If you have sales data split by store and web, share it. The recommendation will then rest on your own numbers and not on general assumptions. Growth's goals for next year would help too, such as revenue, profit, or new customers. The right answer can change depending on which of those they care about most.
growth asked me if we should push store or web next year, not sure where to start

So growth wants a steer on store versus web for next year, and you'd be the one bringing them an answer. Before we pick a starting point, what would "pushing" a channel mean for them in practice? For example, moving marketing budget, investing in the stores or the site, or something else. And what choice are they trying to make with it?

Mostly the marketing money. There's extra budget for next year and they need to decide whether it goes to the stores or the web shop. That's the call in January. I can model it, I'm just not sure how to frame it for them.

That helps: the extra marketing budget, stores or web shop, decided in January. I'd frame it for growth as "where would the next unit of marketing money earn more?", not "which channel is bigger today", because the two can point in different directions. What you can show depends on your data, so what do you have on each channel? For example, sales and margin by channel, and any record of past marketing spend that you can match to sales in stores and on the web.

Orders and returns are in BigQuery, split by channel, store and month. I'd have to check whether we have marketing spend history, I'm not sure. I haven't uploaded anything yet. Not sure how to turn it into something growth can use.

Money after returns is a sensible working measure, and you can tell growth it's the one you're starting with, so they can correct it if they care about something else. transcript.text: Our on-time delivery rate fell from 94% to 88% after we introduced a new route plan in August. Operations wants to know whether to roll the plan back. I have the delivery logs but haven't sent them. How should we approach this?

Your question has two parts. The first is whether the drop from 94% to 88% was caused by the new route plan. The second is whether rolling it back would fix it. Other things may have changed in August, such as seasonal volume, staffing, weather, or the mix of delivery areas. A good approach compares like with like before deciding.

I can help in a few ways. Pick whichever fits best.

I've listed three ways to start. Tell me which one you'd like, and send the delivery logs if you pick the analysis.

choices.title: Business brief on the rollback decision
choices.what: Work through whether the new route plan caused the drop and whether to roll it back. It would weigh the evidence and lay out a recommendation for Operations.

choices.title: Analyze the delivery logs
choices.what: Once you send the logs, I'd measure on-time rates before and after August. I'd break them down by route, area, driver or depot, and time period to see where the drop is concentrated.

choices.title: Guidance on how to approach it
choices.what: A written explanation of how to test whether a route change caused a drop in on-time delivery. It covers what to compare, what else to rule out, and how to frame the decision. It involves no data work.

transcript.text: I'd pick option 2, but I want the method agreed before I send the file. The logs cover January to October and have delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned time, delivered time, weather flag and driver id. I can derive driver tenure from the driver ids, which matters because new drivers also came in August. I don't yet know whether the new plan was rolled out to all depots and routes at the same time. If it was staggered, or applied to some routes and not others, I'd compare treated and untreated routes over the same weeks, a difference-in-differences setup. If not, I'd check Jan to July for a pre-trend first and then model on-time status with weather, driver tenure and holiday weeks as controls. Operations needs a clear answer, so I'd like a first read by depot within the week, with the caveat stated plainly if the data can't separate the plan from the driver change.

It will help if the logs include these columns:
- The delivery date.
- Whether each delivery was on time, or the promised and actual delivery times.
- The route, area, depot or driver.

Once I have them, I'll compare on-time rates before and after the August change. I'll also break the results down to see whether the drop is concentrated in particular routes or areas, or spread across all of them. That will show whether the new plan looks responsible or something else changed at the same time.

Our on-time delivery rate fell from 94% to 88% after we introduced a new route plan in August. Operations wants to know whether to roll the plan back. I have the delivery logs but haven't sent them. How should we approach this?

Here's what I understood: on-time delivery fell from 94% to 88% after the August route plan, and Operations needs to decide whether to roll it back. The real question underneath is whether the plan *caused* the drop, or whether something else changed around the same time. The answer depends a lot on how the plan was introduced. Did it go live everywhere at once, or only on some routes, depots or drivers while others stayed on the old plan? And did anything else change around August, such as volume, season or staffing?

Thanks, that helps. I'm not certain yet whether the plan went live everywhere at once or in stages. I'd need to check with ops, and I can't rule out a partial rollout. What I do know is that August also brought holiday traffic and a batch of new drivers, so those are the two confounders I'm most worried about. I have delivery logs from January to October with delivery id, date, depot, route id, planned time, delivered time, a weather flag and driver id. I haven't sent them yet because I want to be sure about the approach first. The director needs an answer within two weeks. My plan is to compare pre- and post-August on-time rates, adjust for weather, driver tenure and depot, and see whether the drop is concentrated on routes that actually switched to the new plan. Does that sound like the right direction? And is there a record of which routes or depots got the plan and when?

Your direction is sound, with two caveats. 1. **Switched vs. not-switched routes is your strongest test.** A before/after comparison adjusted for weather, tenure and depot can't fully separate the plan from holiday traffic and new drivers if the plan hit everything on the same date. Comparing routes that switched with routes that didn't, over the same weeks, controls for August itself. That only works if the rollout was partial. 2. **The logs as you describe them can't answer your second question.** They have route id and depot, but no column says which routes were on the new plan or from when. That record would sit with ops or whoever owns route planning. The useful version is a list of route ids or depots with the date each one moved to the new plan. - Driver tenure isn't a column either, only driver id. We could estimate it from each driver's first delivery in the logs, but anyone hired before January would look new. Hire dates from ops or HR would be better if they exist. - Check whether the new plan changed the planned times. If it did, "on time" is being measured against a different yardstick before and after. Before you go back to ops, I want to confirm what the director needs. Is it a verdict on whether the plan itself caused the drop, with how confident we can be, rather than just a description of the drop? If the rollout turns out to be all at once, we'd give a best estimate with its limits instead of a clean yes or no. Does that match what Operations expects?

Yes, the director wants a verdict: roll back or keep the plan. She'll accept a best estimate with stated uncertainty, but she needs a recommendation she can act on, not a description of the drop. So I want to know what I can and can't say with confidence before I send anything. On the rollout: I don't know yet whether it went live everywhere at once or in stages. I'll ask ops for the list of route ids or depots with the date each moved to the new plan. If it was all at once, I'd want to know if there's any comparison group at all, like a depot or region that stayed on the old plan for some reason. Without one, I can't separate the plan from holiday traffic and the new drivers, and I'd have to tell her that. Two things I can check myself from the logs before I speak to ops again: whether planned times changed around August, which would mean we're measuring against a different yardstick, and whether the drop is spread across all depots and drivers or concentrated in a few. If it's concentrated, that tells us a lot. For driver tenure, I only have driver ids, so I'd estimate it from first appearance in the logs. Should we re-baseline on the new plan's planned times, or compare delivered time against the old plan's window?
